title: Task Fidelity Scaling Laws — Kobie Crawdord, Snorkel

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 78%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central thesis is that task quality equals data quality in agentic contexts, with empirical evidence showing a 5x RL training uplift from high-quality tasks. The quality criteria and annotation methodology are presented as general principles applicable across agentic task types rather than tied to one vertical. The talk spans data labeling with human and LLM judges, curation via accept/reject criteria, an RL training experiment, and benchmark evaluation analysis. Prerequisites include familiarity with RL training, agentic task environments, and terminal-bench-style frameworks. A conference research presentation with controlled experiments and quantitative findings. A controlled RL experiment holding model, compute, and task count constant provides quantitative evidence of a 5x quality uplift.

summary: Kobe Crawford from Snorkel presents research on task fidelity scaling laws, examining how task quality impacts training outcomes for agentic terminal-bench-style tasks. Snorkel, originating from a Stanford AI research lab and founded in 2019, maintains a core thesis that data quality is critical, which Crawford frames as equivalent to task quality in agentic contexts. The research defines four task-quality criteria: achievable, non-trivial, functionally correct, and environment reliable. Tasks passing all four are accepted; others rejected. Using Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Codex models, accepted tasks averaged twice as many tool calls, lower pass rates, and more output tokens, indicating genuinely harder problems. Failure mode analysis revealed accepted tasks produced cleaner failures tied to genuine difficulty useful for hill climbing, while rejected tasks failed due to under-specification—testable outcomes not clearly specified upfront, tests expecting unrequested things, or implicit dependencies missing from model context. An RL training run with identical model, compute, and task count showed low-quality tasks improved the base model by 1% while high-quality tasks achieved 6%, a 5x uplift difference. In extended Q&A, Crawford discussed how incompletable tasks in public benchmarks create noise that masks model improvement measurement. He acknowledged real-world problem solving involves iteration but emphasized benchmarking requires verifiable outcomes, with the goal that learned skills transfer to unverifiable contexts. Future work includes less verifiable domains beyond coding and math, an open benchmark grants program partnering with external developers, and evaluations involving human-centric dimensions with multiple acceptable outcomes scored on a spectrum. Snorkel's annotation approach combines human annotators and LLM judges using rubric-based criteria, with inter-annotator agreement tested between humans and between LLM judges and humans as part of quality assessment.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Snorkel Background
sections.summary: Kobe Crawford introduces himself as a developer advocate at Snorkel, the frontier AI data lab. He describes Snorkel's origins from a Stanford AI research lab, its founding in 2019, and its core thesis that data quality is critical. He frames the talk around how task quality affects training outcomes in agentic contexts, treating task quality and data quality as largely the same thing.

sections.title: Task Quality Definition and Acceptance Criteria
sections.summary: Crawford defines task quality through four criteria: the task is achievable, non-trivial, functionally correct, and the environment is reliable. Tasks passing all four are accepted; others are rejected. He emphasizes that while architecture and harness changes matter, data quality remains central. The research aims to provide empirical evidence, not just assert the thesis.

sections.title: Accepted vs Rejected Task Comparison
sections.summary: Using Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Codex (GPT-5.2, 5.1, sometimes 4.0), the team compared task completions. Accepted tasks averaged twice as many tool calls, lower pass rates, and more output tokens, indicating genuinely harder problems requiring more reasoning and external tool engagement.

sections.title: Failure Mode Analysis
sections.summary: Failures were categorized to distinguish meaningful failures (model not reaching logical conclusions) from degenerate cases (environmental problems no model could solve). Accepted tasks showed cleaner failures tied to genuine difficulty—useful for hill climbing—while rejected tasks had failures from spec-test mismatches or missing implicit dependencies. Logic errors and incomplete tasks showed reversal patterns between the two buckets.

sections.title: Training Experiment and Results
sections.summary: An RL training run with identical model, compute, and task count compared high-quality vs low-quality tasks. Low-quality tasks improved the base model by ~1%; high-quality tasks improved it by ~6%, yielding a 5x uplift difference. Crawford attributes Snorkel's quality to expert-in-the-loop data generation at scale.

sections.title: Conclusion, Links, and Q&A Introduction
sections.summary: Crawford shares links to Snorkel's research page and benchmarks, including a genetic coding benchmark for terminal-bench-style tasks. A Q&A begins with a question about whether rejected tasks mixed with accepted tasks pull down performance; Crawford indicates he does not have a direct answer from this analysis but references observations from surveying and working with the data.

sections.title: Q&A: Benchmark Noise and Incompletable Tasks
sections.summary: Crawford discusses internal analysis comparing public benchmarks including terminal-bench variants and WeBench. He explains that certain tasks never get completed because they literally cannot be, creating noise that masks whether models are actually improving. This task-quality issue obscures real model improvement signals in benchmark evaluations.

sections.title: Q&A: Under-specification and Input Prescriptiveness
sections.summary: Crawford confirms under-specification is a primary rejection reason: desired testable outcomes are not clearly specified in the test definition upfront, but backend tests expect things never requested. He also describes implicit dependencies in testing that tasks fail to specify, leaving the model without the context needed to approach those dependencies.

sections.title: Q&A: Iteration vs. Verifiable Outcomes
sections.summary: An audience member notes real-world problem solving involves iteration, not one-shot completion, questioning whether classifying incomplete tasks as failures is appropriate. Crawford agrees but explains benchmarking tasks are designed to be verifiable, with the principle that skills learned from verifiable tasks should transfer to unverifiable, iterative real-world contexts.

sections.title: Q&A: Future Challenges and Non-Verifiable Domains
sections.summary: Crawford describes future work targeting less verifiable domains beyond coding and math. Snorkel has an open benchmark grants program partnering with external developers on evaluations in fuzzy, human-centric areas including emotional dimensions, where multiple acceptable outcomes are scored on a spectrum rather than pass/fail.

sections.title: Q&A: Inter-Annotator Agreement and Closing
sections.summary: Crawford explains Snorkel's annotation approach: combining human annotators and LLM judges using rubric-based criteria with longer lists of data points and conditions. Inter-annotator agreement is tested between humans and between LLM judges and humans, forming part of quality assessment. This guiding principle applies across domains, including the explicitly verifiable tests in this study.
